What does a flood protection standard mean?

A protection standard is the return period of the flood a defence is designed to withstand, for example a 1-in-100 standard. Floods above that level overtop or breach the defence, and the damage behind it can be severe because people and assets concentrate there. The standard describes design, not guarantee: defences degrade, the climate moves, and the standard in a global database may not match what is actually in place at a site.

How well does the air-quality record match real monitors?

It was checked against about sixty-five ground monitors for one year. The regional model follows the day-to-day changes only moderately, and its yearly average lay within thirty percent of the monitor at roughly two thirds of unseen sites. What is an internal or shadow carbon price?

A shadow price is a value per tonne of carbon dioxide that a company uses inside its own decisions, such as investment appraisal, even where no tax or market price applies. It tests whether a project stays viable if carbon becomes costly. It differs from a market price, which is what a trading scheme sets today, and from the social cost of carbon, which estimates the economic damage of an extra tonne and is used mainly in public-policy analysis.

A wind energy company with turbines in the North Sea off Denmark and the Netherlands asks for a premium. How is it set?

The engine builds the storm and wave hazard at each turbine site from ERA5 and the ocean-wave reanalysis, with return levels and the share of time vessels can reach the site, which sets how long a repair waits. With no claims supplied, the engine withholds the premium and shows only the weather component, because a premium without those losses would be a false low number. What is TVaR and why report it as well as a return-period loss?

Tail value at risk (TVaR) at 99% is the average loss in the worst 1% of years. A return-period loss only marks where the tail begins; TVaR describes how bad the tail is once you are in it. Two portfolios can share the same 1-in-100 loss while one has a far fatter tail beyond it. Regulators and rating agencies increasingly look at TVaR because it responds to extreme years that a single percentile ignores, and because it behaves better when combining risks.
